title: Quasiparticle-induced transitions in a fluxonium qubit
authors: Maksim Litskevich, Kesavan Manivannan, Benjamin Byrd, Pavel D. Kurilovich, Vladislav D. Kurilovich, Gianluigi Catelani, Ivan V. Pechenezhskiy
abstract: Quasiparticles are a prominent decoherence source in superconducting qubits, but their effects are notoriously difficult to isolate in fluxonium. Unlike a transmon, fluxonium is insensitive to offset charge, precluding charge-parity detection of quasiparticle tunneling. We address this challenge by measuring the excitation and de-excitation rates in a fluxonium qubit under controlled on-chip quasiparticle injection. We show that to accurately model the external magnetic flux dependence of the quasiparticle-induced transition rates, it is necessary to account for the superconducting gap asymmetry across the Josephson junctions. A comparison between theory and experiment constrains the relative quasiparticle contributions of the junction array and the small junction and helps explain previously reported discrepancies between the bounds on the quasiparticle densities inferred for these two circuit elements.
summary: This paper investigates how quasiparticle tunneling causes decoherence in fluxonium qubits. The authors overcome the challenge of charge insensitivity by measuring excitation and de-excitation rates under controlled QP injection. They show that incorporating superconducting gap asymmetry ($\delta\Delta$) into the theory is necessary to reconcile experimental measurements with theoretical predictions regarding the relative contributions of different junction elements.
main_problem: The primary challenge is isolating and quantifying quasiparticle (QP)-induced decoherence effects in fluxonium qubits, a platform difficult to analyze because it lacks the charge sensitivity of transmon qubits.
main_result: By incorporating superconducting gap asymmetry ($\delta\Delta$) into the theoretical model, the authors reconcile discrepancies between previously inferred QP densities from different circuit elements (junction array vs. small junction).
method: The study combines controlled on-chip quasiparticle injection experiments with detailed theoretical modeling of transition rates derived from the qubit Hamiltonian.
model_or_system: The system is a fluxonium qubit, modeled by an anharmonic Josephson junction circuit. The analysis focuses on how QP tunneling affects energy relaxation ($\Gamma_{\downarrow}$) and excitation ($\Gamma_{\uparrow}$) rates as a function of external magnetic flux bias.
key_observables: QP-induced energy relaxation/excitation rates ($\Delta\Gamma_{\downarrow}$), the dependence of these rates on external magnetic flux ($\Phi_{	ext{ext}}$), and the relative contributions from the junction array and small junction.
important_parameters: Superconducting gap asymmetry ($\delta\Delta$), characteristic QP energy width ($\delta E_{	ext{qp}}$), and operating regimes like Integer/Half-Integer Flux Quantum ($	ext{IFQ}/	ext{HFQ}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis requires accounting for the superconducting gap asymmetry across Josephson junctions to accurately model flux dependence, contradicting previous simplifying assumptions.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the external flux dependence of transition rates, comparing background vs. post-injection measurements at IFQ and HFQ, demonstrating how $\delta\Delta$ affects rate suppression.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the difficulty in measuring QP effects in fluxonium. It then develops a theoretical framework to separate contributions from different junction elements using measured transition rates ($\Gamma_{if}$). Finally, it uses experimental measurements across varying magnetic fluxes to constrain the relative roles of these components.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses decoherence mechanisms in superconducting qubits by providing a detailed physical mechanism (gap asymmetry) that can be engineered to suppress environmental noise sources like quasiparticles, which is crucial for scaling quantum processors.
